newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BT says protected against MCI woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BT says protected against MCI woes.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc insisted on Monday that it could protect its shareholders if a troubled $20 billion merger planned with America's MCI Communications Corp needs to be re-negotiated.
Confusion has mounted amid speculation that BT might have limited room to manoeuvre despite an unexpectedly hefty profit warning from MCI last week which sent shares in both companies tumbling.
Sources close to MCI, which has a reputation for not shying away from court action, have been quoted by newspapers as saying that the terms of the original merger do not allow BT to reopen talks.
But a BT spokeswoman told Reuters the company had the "legal protection" needed for its shareholders.

Although MCI told BT in March it expected higher losses than previously forecast because of problems breaking into $100 billion local U.S. markets, BT says it was surprised and disappointed by the scale of the profit warning announced at an MCI board meeting last Wednesday.
MCI said it expected investments in its expanding local telecoms business to ring up $800 million losses this year -- double previous estimates -- and possibly more next year.

BT -- caught between institutional investors who want a new deal to take into account the fall in MCI's shares and between U.S. arbitrageurs who want terms unchanged to save them from multi-billion dollar losses -- declines to comment on the merger's future.

But finance director Robert Brace, MCI's chief executive Gerald Taylor and chairman Bert Roberts on Sunday left London for MCI's headquarters in Washington to spearhead a thorough review of the merger as well as MCI's investment plans and general businesses.

BT's chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield, who was accused by BT shareholders at an annual meeting last week of not having done his homework ahead of the deal, is scheduled to join the group later this week.
Asked why he was delaying his departure, the BT spokeswoman said: "He has other things to do as well."

The British telephone giant, which even before MCI's profit warning was prepared to pay a hefty premium for the 80 percent of MCI it did not already own, has seen its value slide 13 percent over the last 11 days.

Its shares, which have tumbled from a closing high of 502p earlier this month, fell another three percent to 416p on Monday. Stripping out a 35p special dividend due in August, BT's shares are trading around 12p higher than when the MCI merger was announced last November.
Analysts say a disparity of around 17 percent in the BT and MCI share prices signals that investors anticipate rejigged terms more in BT's favour.

James McCafferty, analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett, said that instead of the equivalent of 5.4 BT shares plus $6 for each MCI share, MCI shareholders could receive 4.4 BT shares plus $6. Others say BT should revise terms down to 4.1 shares, implying an MCI share price of $34.
MCI's shares started trade at just above $32 on Monday.
Some analysts are beginning to predict that the longer the review takes, the greater the previously slim odds that BT might attempt to abandon the merger altogether.

However, BT -- which last May walked away from a much bigger merger with Britain's second biggest telecom carrier Cable and Wireless Plc -- stresses that its relationship with MCI remains of key strategic importance.

BT and MCI had planned to create a global giant called Concert Plc, now dubbed "Discord" by some commentators, to sell communications services to high-margin, multinational, corporate customers around the world.
In the meantime, BT says it will complete the review as speedily as possible but can give no guidelines.
"We are conscious that people are looking for more information and as soon as we have that we can tell them...It will take as long as it takes," the spokeswoman said.
